claims.text: Increasing Cr content in steel promotes formation of a Cr-enriched passive oxide film.
Suitable post-thermal treatments promote formation of a dense, uniform, and adherent passive film.
The protective film consists primarily of Cr2O3 together with associated spinel oxides.
Baseline low-to-moderate-Cr steels produced by standard fabrication have thinner, non-uniform, and weakly protective oxide layers.
Minor additions of other alloying elements may stabilize the protective oxide.
The corrosion-controlling structural mediator is a continuous, defect-free, Cr-enriched passive film containing mixed oxide or spinel phases.
Selective oxidation of Cr during exposure forms a protective Cr2O3-rich layer.
A dense Cr2O3 passive film suppresses further corrosion by acting as a barrier to aggressive chemical species.
The Cr-rich passive film minimizes pitting corrosion.
The passive film protects against radiation-induced damage.
Cr-enhanced, thermally treated steels will have higher electrochemical impedance than baseline steels.
Cr-enhanced, thermally treated steels will have higher pitting potentials than baseline steels.
Cr-enhanced, thermally treated steels will have lower corrosion current densities than baseline steels.
XPS and SEM will reveal a denser and more uniform passive film on the modified samples.
The proposed mechanism applies broadly to steels and related alloys in chemical-processing and nuclear-power corrosive environments.
The mechanism may cease to apply under extreme radiation flux or conditions favoring alternative oxide-formation pathways.
Cr is the dominant contributor to passivity, while Ni and Co have more limited effects.
The controlled study compares a Cr-enhanced, thermally treated group against a standard-composition, untreated control under otherwise matched environmental conditions.
Failure to obtain statistically significant improvement in impedance, pitting potential, or passive-film density and uniformity would falsify the proposed hypothesis.
